title: What are the Vector API (SIMD, incubator), Key Derivation Function API (JEP 510), PEM encodings (JEP 470), and KEM API (JEP 452)?
shortTitle: Vector API (SIMD), KDF API, PEM encoding, KEM API — performance and security additions

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** (1) VECTOR API (incubator) — express data-parallel operations that compile to CPU SIMD instructions (AVX-512, NEON). Process 8/16 integers in one instruction instead of one. For: financial calculations, ML, image processing. (2) KEY DERIVATION FUNCTION API (JEP 510) — standard API for deriving cryptographic keys from passwords/secrets using HKDF, PBKDF2. (3) PEM ENCODING (JEP 470) — read/write certificates, keys, CRLs in PEM format (the text format with `-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----`). (4) KEM API (JEP 452) — Key Encapsulation Mechanism for post-quantum cryptography key exchange.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Vector API = the bank's calculator processing 8 transactions at once instead of one-by-one. KDF API = generating secure vault passwords from master keys. PEM encoding = reading security certificates in the standard text format. KEM API = quantum-resistant key exchange for future-proof encryption.

**One line to remember:** Vector API = SIMD parallel math (incubator). KDF = key derivation (HKDF). PEM = certificate format API. KEM = post-quantum key exchange. All specialized — know they exist, don't need deep details.

sections.s2_technical:
Recent JDKs added performance and security APIs. The Vector API (incubating, JEP series) exposes SIMD — single instruction, multiple data — so a loop over an array of numbers compiles to hardware vector instructions that process several lanes at once, speeding up bulk numeric work like risk calculations across many positions.

On the security side: the KDF API (Key Derivation Function, JEP 478) provides a standard way to derive keys (e.g. HKDF) for encrypting sensitive banking data. PEM Encoding support standardises reading and writing PEM-format keys and certificates used in TLS and signing. The KEM API (Key Encapsulation Mechanism, JEP 452) supports modern, post-quantum-ready key exchange, letting two parties agree on a shared secret securely.

A banking example: using the Vector API to compute portfolio risk over thousands of positions in parallel lanes, the KDF API to derive per-session encryption keys, PEM support to load the TLS certificate, and KEM for forward-secure key exchange with a partner bank. Senior nuance: the Vector API is about throughput on CPU-bound numeric code and still incubating, so gate it behind benchmarks; the security APIs standardise what used to require third-party crypto libraries, reducing dependency risk in regulated environments.
sections.s3_banking: Problem — Portfolio risk over thousands of positions was CPU-bound and slow, and key derivation/exchange relied on ad-hoc third-party crypto libraries in a regulated bank. Fix: the Vector API processes positions in SIMD lanes for throughput, while the standard KDF, PEM, and KEM APIs provide audited key derivation, certificate handling, and forward-secure key exchange without extra dependencies.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** Input: positions with quantities [100, 50] and prices [2450.5, 3100.0].

**Step 2.** The Vector API would load several quantity/price pairs into SIMD lanes and multiply them in one hardware instruction per lane group.

**Step 3.** Lane-wise, position 1 yields 100×2450.5=245050 and position 2 yields 50×3100=155000.

**Step 4.** Alongside, the KDF derives a session key, PEM loads the TLS cert, and KEM establishes a forward-secure shared secret with the partner bank.

**Step 5.** The risk array [245050.0, 155000.0] is produced with higher throughput, and the crypto uses standard audited APIs.

```text
INFO: risk=[245050.0, 155000.0] (SIMD lanes); keys via KDF/KEM, cert via PEM
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
These are specialized APIs: Vector API enables SIMD parallel computation (8-16 operations per instruction — useful for financial batch calculations). KDF API standardizes key derivation from passwords/secrets (HKDF, PBKDF2). PEM encoding API reads/writes the standard text certificate format (`-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----`). KEM API provides post-quantum-safe key exchange (Kyber). In interviews, mention their existence and purpose — deep details are only needed for specialized roles (performance engineering, security).
